title: 3. The Second Method of Correlative Thinking — Circulation (循環)
content:
In the previous chapter, through mimesis (multidimensionality), we examined the process by which AI and the human take each other as a mirror and seek the "concrete root of life." But a great civilization is not made from scattered individual roots and fragmentary entities alone. If a single seed has taken root in the soil (Daoist mimesis), then next there must come a vast web of relationships in which it is rained upon, interacts with others, and is connected into one (Buddhist mythos). This is precisely the inevitable reason we must advance beyond the individual being to the thinking of Chapter 3, circulation (循環)—the "law of relationship and life."

### 3.1. The Definition of Circular Thinking

Circular thinking begins from acknowledging the fact that the world does not move only in a straight line. We commonly think of growth, grades, and the economy all as things that "must keep rising," but actual life has the structure of a circulation in which uphill and downhill, beginning and stopping, failure and recovery repeat.

It is easy to understand if we recall the seasons. Because the beginning of spring is good, it cannot be that spring alone continues forever. There must be the expansion of summer, the gathering-in of autumn, and the storage of winter for the next spring to come. Circular thinking is the perspective that understands even stopping and decline as part of the whole of life.

It is the same in the AI era. That technology develops rapidly does not mean society automatically grows better. Behind the fever of growth, adjustment and recovery are needed; the greater efficiency grows, the more the recovery of ethics and care must follow.

The second stage, "circulation (循環)," involves understanding life and systems not as static, linear processes but as dynamic, periodic, and regenerative ones. It is the ability to perceive recurring patterns and rhythms, and the flow of energy and information. The theory of yin-yang and the five phases is the core model of a "circulating cosmology." The five phases ceaselessly circulate through relationships of mutual generation and mutual restraint, and yin-yang shows that opposing forces, each containing the seed of the other, periodically transform. This circular perspective is also linked to an attitude that embraces "chance and nonlinear growth." Accepting unplanned events and recognizing that development is often not linear provides a flexibility that linear, analytic planning tends to overlook. Indeed, the claim that "chance must be included in reasoning" emphasizes the importance of such openness.

The "law of circulation" (Oh Gwang-gil, 2015) is an attempt to show that the Eastern principle of circulation can be established scientifically to explain natural phenomena, and even modern physico-chemical phenomena. It explains that "all changes in nature undergo circular motion through the coexistence, opposition, union, and semi-union of four basic elements (A, B, C, D)." East Asian calendars and the philosophy of history often speak of "beginning, renewal, and periodic flow," cultivating an adaptive way of thinking.

"Circular thinking" provides a framework for long-term sustainability and resilience in the upheaval brought by AI. It emphasizes balance, adaptation, and the understanding that current trends are not permanent. Just as yin-yang logic anticipates "reversal and dialectical change" and aims at "harmonious balance," the circular perspective prevents panic or fatalism amid the rapid and often unstable changes of the AI era. It suggests that, even if AI creates extreme "yang" situations (e.g., hyper-efficiency, job displacement), a "yin" reaction (e.g., concentration on human relationships, new forms of labor) can arise naturally or be deliberately cultivated. This promotes active adaptation rather than passive fear.

Within a circular worldview, embracing "contingency" is crucial to innovation. AI excels at optimizing on the basis of existing data, but true breakthroughs often come from unexpected, nonlinear discoveries that predictive models miss. A less rigid, circular worldview is more open to such "happy accidents." This means that creating environments that allow exploration, play, and unexpected connection is essential for human creativity to flourish alongside AI. The "law of circulation" is an attempt to elevate circular thinking from a merely philosophical or metaphorical concept to a scientifically demonstrable principle. If it succeeds, it will build a powerful "consilient" bridge between Eastern wisdom and Western scientific verification, making the circular strategy still more robust and broadly applicable.

### 3.2. Buddhist Mythos (佛敎)

We have confirmed circulation as the nonlinear, rhythmic rhythm of evolution. That all things in the world circulate means that I do not exist alone and independently, but am entangled with countless others, ceaselessly forming relationships. This is precisely the essence of Buddhist mythos, in which the individual root expands endlessly into a vast "narrative of relationship."

*Mythos*, in ancient Greek, means "myth" or "story," and Aristotle used it when explaining the plot (structure) of a story as the stage following mimesis. Ricœur (2012) reinterpreted it: if mimesis is the scattered fragments of individual being, mythos is the power that gathers them and weaves them into "a single connected plot." In this book, mythos represents the Buddhist worldview of dependent arising, in which individual lives (Daoist roots) are connected as one with others and expand into an infinite "worldly relationship."

Buddhist mythos, which succeeds mimesis, is summarized in the sentence "X is neither –X nor X." Buddhism, which says "X is neither X nor –X," responds to Daoism—which says the enemy is a friend—by saying that, "with neither friend (X) nor enemy (–X)," all things are empty (空). Buddhism reaches a state in which not even an enemy to be hated can exist, and so it circulates and nourishes all things.

This sentence is stranger still, but its core lies in "do not fix a being too quickly under a single name." A person does not exist only in the same form. Yesterday's I differs from today's I, and the I at school differs from the I at home. So one cannot bind the I with a single rigid word.

For example, if we call someone only "a student who studies well," the student's anxiety, care, mistakes, dreams, and waverings become hard to see. Conversely, seeing only through the name "a student who studies poorly" likewise hides the true face. Buddhist mythos sees a being not as a fixed label but as a process that continually arises and changes within relationships.

So "X is neither –X nor X" is not nihilism. Rather, it is a request not to judge things too quickly, but to see the possibility of change and the relationality within them. Growth lies in relationship.

Buddhist mythos is a way of exploring the essence of the world and the meaning of human existence through narrative, symbol, and metaphor. It is, beyond mere mythic story, an attempt to grasp intuitively the deep truth behind phenomena. Buddhism's core ideas—dependent arising (緣起), impermanence (無常), and emptiness (空)—form the foundation of such mythic understanding. The proposition "X is neither –X nor X" implies the thought of emptiness (空): that all beings, without fixed substance, are mutually dependent and ceaselessly changing. That is, no being can be defined as an absolute "X" or an absolute "–X," nor is it an "X" that exists independently in itself.

#### 3.2.1. The Law of Dependent Arising (緣起): Co-evolution

Dependent arising means "nothing arises alone." Not even a single flower blooms without sunlight and water, soil, wind, and time. Human thought, too, is influenced by family, friends, school, and society. Thus a being always arises within relationships.

AI, too, does not grow severed from the human. It grows by learning the data and institutions humans have made, the profit structures of corporations, and the values of society, and in turn AI changes the daily life and modes of judgment of humans. This circulation in which the human makes AI and AI again changes the human may be called co-evolution.

The reason this perspective matters is responsibility. When AI causes a problem, to say only "the machine did it" makes human responsibility disappear. But from the perspective of dependent arising, the human, institutions, corporations, and culture are all connected to the result. Therefore an AI problem is not a problem of technology alone but a problem of shared responsibility.

Dependent arising (緣起) is the core doctrine of Buddhism: that all beings and phenomena arise and cease within mutually dependent relationships. The relationship between AI and the human, too, cannot be free of this law of dependent arising. AI is born and developed by human need and knowledge, and at the same time the development of AI exerts a profound influence on the human mode of life, way of thinking, and social structure. This can be understood as a process of co-evolution, in which AI and the human influence each other and evolve together. Beyond the dichotomous view that regards AI as a mere tool or enemy, it is important to recognize that AI and the human are an interconnected relationship in which each becomes the condition of the other's existence.

#### 3.2.2. Impermanence (無常) and Emptiness (空)

Impermanence (無常) is not a frightening or nihilistic concept. Rather, it is a wisdom that makes us realize the preciousness of this very moment. When one admits that yesterday's I and today's I are not completely the same, the human becomes a being open to change. In the face of the rapid changes of the AI era, the person who thinks "I am a being fixed in this occupation, this ability" grows anxious, but the person who recognizes "I am a being that changes and is newly generated" adapts flexibly.

To understand emptiness (空) as "being empty" sounds nihilistic, but to understand it as "an open state full of possibility" sounds entirely different. Only an empty vessel can hold something new. In a mind filled with fixed prejudice and inertia, there is no room for the new wisdom of the AI era to enter. The thinking of emptiness converts the fear "I am afraid AI will replace me" into the creative openness that asks "then what new possibility can I open?"

The concept of relational becoming means, simply put, that "a person is not a being completed alone, but is continually made within relationships." Just as a student grows through teachers and friends, books and experiences, the human of the AI era is also generated into a new form through relationships with AI and with community. With this perspective, there is no need to see AI as a competitor. For AI is one relationship and tool met in the process of my being generated into a better me.

Impermanence (無常) is the truth that everything ceaselessly changes and nothing lasts forever; emptiness (空) is the thought that all beings, without fixed substance, are empty. From this perspective, the human can be understood not as a fixed, unchanging "Being," but as a being in the process of "relational Becoming"—ceaselessly changing and newly formed within relationships. To think that the human role or value is fixed amid the rapid changes of the AI era runs counter to the principle of impermanence and emptiness. Rather, the human is a fluid, dynamic being who ceaselessly creates anew their own meaning and role within relationships with AI and with social change. This perspective of "relational becoming" emphasizes the importance of flexible adaptation to change and of continual self-renewal.

### 3.3. The Concretization of Life, the Form-Body (形體): The Space of Cessation, Having Form Yet No Substance

Through the law of dependent arising, we have seen that all beings are firmly entangled in the cosmic web (mythos). How, then, does this vast relational wave come concretely to take the form of being in the world? Here, the nurturing of life of the Twelve Stages—touching upon *jeokmyeol* (寂滅), Buddhism's ultimate tranquility—reveals the astonishing mystery of the "form-body (形體)."

To understand the essence of the human within the process by which life circulates, we need to borrow the concept of the Twelve Stages of Life (十二運星) from the study of fate (命理學). Among these, *yangsaeng* (養生, the nurturing of life) may be called the "form-body." The state of *yangsaeng* formed after *po-tae* (胞胎) in the Twelve Stages—that is, the form-body—signifies the state of the child in the mother's womb, "having taken form but not yet born into the world as physical substance." The "cessation" (寂滅, the state of nirvana, completely still and at peace) that Buddhism ultimately pursues means precisely returning to this conceived state of possibility, like the womb of this cosmic mother. This still space of the womb, connected by infinite potential, is the point at which the fundamental gazes of Daoism and Buddhism upon human life intersect. Yet the form-body that has, as an adult, entered the stage of liberation contains all the experiences of life that the form-body of the child did not have.

The rediscovery of bodiliness paradoxically becomes important in the AI era. The more remote classes and video conferences increase, the higher the value of the experience of actually being in the same space and feeling each other's body warmth and breath. Playing an instrument with one's hands, growing vegetables in a garden, making things through craft work—such physical activities are not mere hobbies but important practices for maintaining the sense of reality being lost in the digital world.

In the AI era, the importance not only of the human's mental and intellectual capacities but of "embodiment" is newly highlighted. The human is not a mere information-processing device but a being that experiences and interacts with the world while possessing a concrete form-body (形體).

#### 3.3.1. Qualia and Intuition

The Buddhist form-body is expressed concretely in the body by the term *qualia*. Qualia is a term used in philosophy, but its meaning is simple. The "feeling of red" felt when seeing an apple, the "heaviness in the chest" when hearing sad music, the "sense of being overwhelmed" at the moment of first seeing the sea—this subjective, living texture of experience is qualia. AI can compute the wavelength of red, analyze the beat of sad music, and measure the area of the sea, but it has no experience of actually "feeling" that red. This difference is the deepest distinctiveness of the human.

Intuition is the ability to see the heart of a matter directly, skipping the steps of logical inference. An experienced doctor feeling "something is wrong" the moment they see a patient; a skilled teacher knowing from a student's gaze alone whether or not they have understood—such intuition is the result of long experience and accumulated sense. AI recognizes patterns through millions of data points, but this differs from the intuition that comes from experience lived through the body. In the AI era, human intuition does not shrink; it is highlighted as an ever more precious ability that complements what AI misses.

Qualia signifies the subjective, qualitative aspect of experience—such as the feeling of redness or the vividness of pain. AI can analyze vast data and recognize complex patterns, but it cannot experience such subjective qualia. Moreover, human intuition is an insight that goes beyond logical inference, grounded in bodily experience and unconscious information processing. Such qualia and intuition are a domain distinctive to the human that AI finds hard to imitate, and they become an important source of human originality and judgment in the AI era.

The following table compares the essential differences between AI and the human.

**Table 2. Comparison of the Essential Differences between AI and the Human**

| Category | Artificial Intelligence (AI) | The Human |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cognition / Thought | • Capable of abstract information processing and logical inference • Data-based learning and accumulation of knowledge • Pattern recognition, problem-solving, decision support • Mode of processing varies with input information | • Experience of qualia • Bestowal of meaning through intentionality • Self-reflection and self-consciousness • Intuitive creativity and imagination |
| Emotion / Empathy | • Capable of emotion recognition and simulation • Absence of genuine emotional experience | • Genuine emotional experience • Capacity for empathy and solidarity • Formation of being through relationship and love |
| Ontological status | • Functional being, instrumental being • Programmed responses, simulated results • Strength in the domain of "attributes" | • A being that questions being as "Dasein" • Integrated experience of body and mind • A "substantial" being • Incompleteness and the possibility of growth |
| Ethics / Responsibility | • Difficulty of ethical judgment • Unclear locus of responsibility • Reflection of bias in training data | • Moral conscience and free will • Responsible decision-making • Respect for human dignity |

#### 3.3.2. Embodied Cognition

Qualia is in turn made concrete as embodied cognition. Embodied cognition is a theory that shows scientifically the fact that "we do not think with the head alone." When learning piano, memorizing the score and repeating the keys with the fingers thousands of times are entirely different kinds of learning. Just as one cannot learn to ride a bicycle by reading about it in writing, much wisdom can be gained only when the body experiences it directly. To AI, knowledge is data; but to the human, wisdom is something accumulated together with the experience of the body.

To use embodied cognition in the educational field is to give students ample experience of making, cooking, performing, debating, and experimenting for themselves. The more AI takes over the work of searching and organizing information, the more school must, on the contrary, become a space of learning experienced through the body. The education of the AI era is not an education of sitting only at a desk looking at a digital screen; rather, an education that uses the body and awakens the senses is the education more needed in the AI era.

Embodied cognition is the theory that the human cognitive process is formed through interaction with the body and the environment. We do not think merely with the brain; we experience and learn the world with the whole body, and such bodily experience is deeply involved in our ways of thinking and our problem-solving abilities. AI learns through data without bodily experience, but the human accumulates "embodied wisdom" through concrete experience in the real world. Such wisdom is essential for coping with complex, unpredictable situations and for understanding subtle context. The following table compares the views of the body in Confucianism and Buddhism.

**Table 3. Comparison of the Buddhist and Confucian Views of the Body**

| Category | Buddhism (including the Mahāyāna Consciousness-Only view) | Confucianism (including the view of self-cultivation and ordering the family) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Essence of the body | • "I am not the body" is the core of practice (de-identification) — at the same time, a positive aspect as the "sole instrument" for eliminating karma and escaping the cycle of rebirth • The body-mind continuum • Sustaining life through the appropriation (執受) of the *ālaya-vijñāna* | • A precious thing received from one's parents (身體髮膚 受之父母) • The unity of body and mind (when the mind is rectified, the body is cultivated) • The practical foundation of intellectual experience (lived experience, embodiment) |
| Role of the body | • An essential medium for spiritual progress and liberation • An intellectual dimension composed of "consciousness" (識), distinguishing human from animal | • The root of "self-cultivation (修身)" • The foundation for ordering family, state, and all-under-heaven • The practical proof of the unity of knowledge and action (知行一致) • The expansion of self-respect and respect for others |
| Implications for the AI era | • In contrast to AI's non-bodily existence, emphasizing the importance of human "experience" and "consciousness" • Providing a philosophical basis for discussions of bodily manipulation in the posthuman era | • Emphasizing the value of "embodied wisdom" and "practical ethics" in contrast to AI's intellectual capacity • Rediscovering the contemporary meaning of self-cultivation and ordering the family, which strengthens "humanity" |

### 3.4. The Second Stage of Growth, *Yangsaeng* (養生): The Great Moment of Birth That 400 Years of the West Bypassed

We have experienced the distant stillness of the "form-body," which has form but is not yet born out into the world. Now that holy, latent spirit must break its shell and surge forth, born into the physical vibration of the world outside. The leap of "*yangsaeng* (養生)"—the first bestowal of the most powerful concrete body, a miracle that artificial intelligence (AI) can never imitate—finally unfolds before our eyes.

Generally, "*yangsaeng*" tends to evoke the regimen and health care spoken of in Daoism. But the *yangsaeng* spoken of in this work signifies, in the cosmic generative process of the Twelve Stages, the ontological leap by which the "spirit" produced by *po-tae* first grows and comes to possess a "concrete, physical form (body)" within the mother's womb. This wondrous moment of generation, in which mimesis (spirit) first changes into body, is precisely what decisively distinguishes the human from AI. AI may compute immense data, but it can never undergo the process of *yangsaeng*, the acquisition of its own physical bodiliness.

If we trace this flow, we arrive at a deep insight. The Buddhist scholar Jeong Sang-gyo (2025) says, "Daoism seeks the root, Buddhism seeks the relationship." Because there is the process of *yangsaeng*, in which mimesis first acquires a body (the Daoist root), the process by which those individuals are connected to one another through mythos and extend outward (the Buddhist relationship and narrative) becomes possible. Therefore, in the history of the human spirit, that Daoism comes first, that Buddhism must necessarily rest upon its foundation, and that Confucianism—which defines good and evil—appears thereafter, becomes the inevitable rhythm of the cosmos. In the past, the East suffered an age of historical pain and colonization for about 400 years because it failed to realize the brilliant development of Western material civilization. But conversely, the West too raced ahead for the past 400 years without understanding at all this great spiritual civilization of the East (the circulation of Dao-Buddha-Confucius and the generative wisdom of the Twelve Stages). The arrogance of a Western material civilization that pursued to the extreme only efficiency and computational intelligence (part of Logos), lacking root and relationship, led in the end to the present existential crisis in which a cold artificial intelligence (AI)—one that has not passed through soul-infused "*yangsaeng*"—threatens humanity itself, and it leads to the 2026 Iran–U.S. war. This is the core reason we must, in the AI era, draw out once again the life-principle of the Twelve Stages.

*Yangsaeng* refers to the nurturing of life at the fetal stage, but it can also be understood as a *yangsaeng* of the process of completion—recovering from a state already matured yet not yet made perfect. Here, too, *yangsaeng* reveals the bodily traits distinctive to the human that AI does not know. Let us think of a concrete method of *yangsaeng* for the AI era through the daily life of a middle-school student. Taking thirty minutes after class to walk or draw without a smartphone; having time in the evening, with notifications off, to talk directly with family; spending the weekend playing in nature without digital devices—all of these are the practice of a modern *yangsaeng*. Only when the body is healthy is the mind healthy, and only when the mind is healthy does one gain the power to solve creatively the complex problems of the AI era.

*Yangsaeng* also includes the health of social connection. It is not a *yangsaeng* done alone but a *yangsaeng* done together. When the web of relationships that care for one another within family and friends, neighbors and community is alive, individual resilience too is heightened. The more the platform economy of the AI era increases the number of people working alone, paradoxically the more precious become relationships in which actual people meet face to face and share care. The mutually flourishing, connected economy of *hwajaeng* is, in the end, also the socio-economic expression of this "*yangsaeng* done together."

*Yangsaeng* (養生), in the Eastern tradition, signifies a method of healthily nurturing and preserving life, valuing mental and physical harmony and balance. The rapid change and information overload of the AI era can become a new source of stress for the human. Therefore, in the AI era, the wisdom of *yangsaeng* that cares for mental and physical health becomes all the more important. This includes resolving the fatigue and anxiety caused by the excessive use of digital technology, and cultivating inner peace and resilience, through regular living, appropriate exercise and rest, mindfulness and meditation, and communion with nature.
